title: Sundiata, the Lion of Mali
author: Épopée mandingue
desc: L'enfant qui ne marchait pas devint le fondateur de l'Empire du Mali.

chapters.t: The Boy Who Could Not Walk
p: About eight hundred years ago, in the land of the Mandinka, a king called Naré Maghan had a son. His mother was Sogolon, a woman who was not beautiful but had great powers.
A hunter had made a prophecy: "The son of this woman will be a great king."
The boy's name was Sundiata. But there was a problem. At seven years old, Sundiata could not walk. He crawled on the ground like a baby.
The king's first wife, Sassouma, laughed at him. She wanted her own son to be king. "Look at Sogolon's son!" she said. "He crawls like a snake! This is your great king?"
Every day, Sogolon cried. And every day, Sundiata listened in silence.
One day, Sassouma insulted Sogolon again. She refused to give her baobab leaves for her sauce. "If your son was a man, he would bring you leaves himself!"
That evening, Sundiata said: "Mother, today I will walk."
He asked the blacksmiths to make a huge iron bar. It was so heavy that six men carried it.
Sundiata took the bar. He pushed on it with all his strength. His legs shook. Sweat ran down his face. And slowly, the iron bar bent… and Sundiata stood up.
The griots sang. The people shouted. Sundiata walked to the baobab tree, pulled it out of the ground, and put it in front of his mother's house.
"Mother," he said, "from today, all the women of the village will come to *your* house for leaves."
After the old king died, Sassouma's son became king. Sassouma was afraid of Sundiata. She wanted to kill him.
So Sogolon took her children and left. For many years, they lived in exile, far from home. They went from kingdom to kingdom.
Sundiata grew into a strong young man. He learned to hunt. He learned to fight. He learned how other kings ruled their people. He became wise.
Meanwhile, a terrible sorcerer-king called Soumaoro Kanté attacked the land of the Mandinka. He was cruel and powerful. People said no weapon could kill him.
One day, messengers found Sundiata. "Come back," they begged. "Only you can save us."
Sundiata returned with a great army. Many kings joined him.
But how could he defeat Soumaoro? His sister, Nana Triban, had a secret. She had been Soumaoro's prisoner, and she had discovered his weakness: the spur of a white rooster.

In 1235, at the battle of Kirina, the two armies met. Sundiata put the rooster's spur on an arrow. He shot it. The arrow only scratched Soumaoro. But immediately, his magic disappeared. He ran away into the mountains and was never seen again.
The Mandinka were free.
After the victory, Sundiata gathered all the kings and chiefs in a place called Kurukan Fuga. There, he founded the Empire of Mali.

The kings and chiefs agreed on rules for living together. These rules said that every life is precious, that people must help each other, and that there must be no slavery. Many people call it the Charter of Manden, one of the oldest declarations of human rights in the world.
The Empire of Mali became one of the greatest empires in history. It was rich in gold and famous for its cities, like Niani and later Timbuktu.
Today, griots in Mali, Guinea, Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire still sing the story of Sundiata. They remind children of an important lesson: the weakest child can become the strongest king.
